Build with agents

Start a task, guide the work, and review the result.

Choose your model

Open Settings → Agents → Models.

  • Codex or Claude Code: use Sign in to connect your account. If the CLI is missing or too old, copy the displayed install or upgrade command, run it in your terminal, then choose Check. ByteQuay does not install or update these CLIs itself.
  • Your agent API: choose Add API key, select a supported provider, such as DeepSeek, enter a label and key, then Add key. DeepSeek tasks require Codex CLI, but not a Codex account.
  • Once Ready, choose your Development and Review models. Use repository Model overrides for a different choice.

Keys are stored encrypted on your Mac. Saved OpenAI keys cannot run agent tasks yet. Installing a CLI or saving a key alone is not enough: the CLI must meet the required version, and the selected account or key must have an available model. Today and Assistant use the global Development selection; an account available only to one repository cannot enable them.

New agent actions stay hidden until the selected agent and model are usable. Existing tasks, reviews, and notices remain available.

Keep Claude Code accounts separate

Use multiple accounts with isolated sign-ins and sessions.

  1. In Models → Claude accounts, choose Add Claude account. Enter a name and email, then Add and sign in.
  2. Select the account for Development or Review. Global accounts are available across repositories.
  3. For a dedicated account, add it in the repository’s Model overrides, or choose Use only here on a global account. Other repositories cannot use it.

Changing defaults affects new tasks. Existing tasks keep their selected account.

Start an agent task

  1. Open Tasks → + New task and choose a ready model.
  2. Describe the outcome, useful context, and how to check success.
  3. Review Automation, then Send. ByteQuay prepares a separate branch and working copy.

Steer adds guidance when supported; Run next queues a message. Stop this turn interrupts the agent.

Review approvals, inspect WorkBench → Changes, and check tests before Mark it complete.

Check limits in Usage. Add reusable instructions in Settings → Agents → Skills.

Deliver changes and repair CI

The composer’s automation chip shows one icon for each step a new task will take. Click it and drag the slider to choose how far the task goes; each step includes the ones before it:

  • Auto-Commit: commits finished work on the task’s branch. Nothing leaves your Mac.
  • Auto-Draft PR: pushes commits and creates or updates a draft PR.
  • CI fix: watches CI beside the task after each push. It reruns flaky jobs and repairs failures the PR caused. Failures that also fail on the base branch are left alone until the next push. Once every check passes, it marks the draft PR ready for review. CI repair agent follows Development unless you choose another supported agent.
  • Auto-Review fix: gives new comments on the PR’s open review threads to the task’s agent. It fixes what it agrees with and explains what it doesn’t. Once the fix is pushed, ByteQuay posts each reply and resolves the threads that were fixed. A thread gets at most three rounds.
  • Auto-merge: once the PR can merge, waits for the delay in Settings → Agents → Workflow (one hour unless you change it), then rebase-merges it or joins the merge queue. GitHub decides whether the PR can merge; the task’s CI fix must also pass and no review thread may be open.

The reset button returns to your saved default. A task’s automation is fixed once it starts: its chip then shows each step as done (green), running (yellow), not started (grey) or needing you (red); hover a step for details. Every step after Auto-Commit can write to GitHub. Change the default for new tasks during setup or in Settings → Agents → Workflow. Automatic repairs and fixes use your model allowance.

The pill above the composer says what automation is doing now. Its stop square stops automation and keeps your draft; while a merge counts down, it cancels the merge and the PR stays open.

You can keep sending messages while CI Autofix watches. A message stops a repair in progress, and your next turn starts from the fixes CI already pushed. The pill’s stop square ends the current CI run; the next push starts another.

CI monitoring runs locally while ByteQuay is open, has no time limit, and resumes after a restart. ByteQuay notifies you when failures already fail on the base branch, when three repairs don’t make CI pass, or when a repair needs your input.

Cherry-pick and backport

Link related repositories once in repository settings under Related workspaces. A Fork means your code builds on that repository, so Fork links form a repo line, such as an open-source project, its internal fork, and a product built on that fork. Every workspace in the line shows it, and agents can read and start work anywhere in it.

  1. In Commits → History, choose a repository upstream in the repo line. Select commits, or open Pull requests and pick a merged one.
  2. Choose Cherry-pick. Check the plan with Dry run, then Start cherry-pick. Starting allows ByteQuay to push the work branch, open a draft pull request, push CI fixes, and rebase when the target moves.
  3. Open the task from the toast, or from Tasks → Cherry-pick. The agent resolves conflicts, then builds and tests the touched modules. Every repair is a separate fixup commit right after the commit it belongs to. Stages, Commits, and CI checks on the right show where it stands; message the agent at any time, and it reads your message at its next step.
  4. When CI is green, choose Approve squash to fold the fixups into their commits. ByteQuay pushes the result and waits for CI again; then choose Merge pull request.

Pause holds the task after its current step, including rebases. Abort closes the pull request and deletes the work branch; the target branch is not touched.

To carry a pull request down the line, pick it and choose Backport, then confirm the repositories to include. Each one gets its own cherry-pick and pull request after the pull request before it merges. Chains show in Commits → Cherry pick of every repository they touch; you can also ask an agent with @backport.
